name: Kangaroo
description: Achilles tendon stores and releases kinetic energy at 93% efficiency. Pendulum gait exploits natural resonance for minimal-energy locomotion. Tail functions as dynamic counterweight. Speed-energy curve inverts: faster travel costs less per distance.

core_attributes.neurology: spring-loaded locomotion cortex, vestibular balance system
core_attributes.pattern: elastic energy storage, pendulum gait resonance, ballistic trajectory optimization

scope.definition: Fraction of mechanical energy recovered from tendon elastic storage during each hopping stride, compared to equivalent muscle-powered stride without tendon recoil contribution.

evidence.source: Alexander & Vernon (1975) 'The mechanics of hopping by kangaroos', Journal of Zoology 177:265-303; Biewener & Baudinette (1995) 'In vivo muscle force and elastic energy storage during steady-speed hopping', Journal of Experimental Biology 198:1829-1841.
cross_domain_examples: red kangaroo gastrocnemius tendon stores 35-40% of stride energy at 6 m/s — metabolic rate independent of speed
human Achilles tendon stores 17% of stride energy at equivalent speed — kangaroo 2× more efficient
locust hindleg tendon: 97% elastic energy recovery during jump — extreme elastic storage specialization
pronghorn antelope: muscle-tendon energy storage enables 95 km/h sustained speed with moderate metabolism

scope.falsifiability: If oxygen consumption per meter traveled increases with hopping speed for kangaroos (as in most mammals), elastic energy storage is not the mechanism enabling speed-independent metabolic rate.
scope.measurement_limits: Elastic storage efficiency is speed-dependent — optimal at 6-8 m/s for red kangaroo. Very slow hops and very fast hops are metabolically expensive. Measurement requires oxygen consumption + kinematic analysis simultaneously.

scope.definition: Energy savings from ballistic flight phase (airborne) of kangaroo hop — fraction of horizontal velocity maintained through aerial phase vs equivalent quadruped gait at same speed.

evidence.source: Baudinette et al. (1992) 'Cost of locomotion in wild tammar wallabies', Journal of Experimental Biology 171:245-255.
cross_domain_examples: kangaroo aerial phase maintains 0.91 of horizontal velocity vs 0.67 for quadruped at same speed
at 6 m/s hopping uses 0.22 ml O2/kg/m vs 0.45 for equivalent quadruped — 51% savings
bipedal jumping robots: ballistic aerial phase provides same velocity-maintenance advantage in flat terrain

scope.falsifiability: If metabolic cost per meter for kangaroos increases proportionally with speed (as for quadrupeds), the ballistic conservation advantage is not operating.
scope.measurement_limits: Savings are terrain-dependent — obstacle-rich or soft-surface terrain eliminates ballistic efficiency advantage. Uphill hopping is energetically expensive; downhill hopping is near-free from potential energy conversion.

scope.definition: Inverted pendulum mechanical efficiency of kangaroo slow quadrupedal gait (pentapedal walk) — fraction of gravitational potential energy recovered as forward kinetic energy per stride.

evidence.source: Dawson & Taylor (1973) 'Energetic cost of locomotion in kangaroos', Nature 246:313-314; Griffin & Kram (2000) 'Penguin waddling is not wasteful', Nature 408:929.
cross_domain_examples: pentapedal walk (tail + forelimbs) at slow speed: mechanical efficiency 0.65-0.70 — lower than hopping
human walking pendulum efficiency 0.65 — analogous inverted pendulum mechanism
walking robot with compliant limbs: 0.68 pendulum efficiency — biological walking achieves similar to engineered

scope.falsifiability: If energy measurement shows pentapedal walking is metabolically cheaper than equivalent-speed quadruped walking, the pendulum mechanism is providing efficiency gains.
scope.measurement_limits: Pentapedal walk (using tail) is used only below ~2 m/s. Above 2 m/s kangaroos switch to hopping. The pentapedal gait efficiency is lower than hopping — it is used for slow maneuvering, not energy efficiency.

scope.definition: Contribution of tail inertia to angular momentum balance during rapid acceleration — measured as fraction of whole-body angular momentum change absorbed by tail during stride initiation.

evidence.source: Askew et al. (2014) 'The kangaroo's tail propels and powers pentapedal locomotion', Biology Letters 10:20140381.
cross_domain_examples: kangaroo tail generates 15-18% of total propulsive force during pentapedal gait — not passive stabilizer
tail removes 30% of rotational impulse during rapid direction change, preventing trunk pitching
cheetah tail: analogous dynamic counterbalance during high-speed turning, absorbing angular momentum

scope.falsifiability: If tail fixation in pentapedal locomotion experiments shows no increase in trunk pitch oscillation during acceleration, the counterbalancing function is not operating.
scope.measurement_limits: Counterbalance function is speed and acceleration dependent. During sustained steady hopping the tail plays a minor stabilizing role; during acceleration and turning its role increases dramatically.
